title: MVP Design
subtitle: The smallest valuable thing you can ship and learn from
useWhen: You're about to spend months building a complete product before getting any customer feedback. You want to launch something real without building everything first, but you're not sure what to cut and what to keep.
howToUse: The Minimum Viable Product concept, popularised by Eric Ries in The Lean Startup, is about finding the smallest version of your product that delivers enough value to attract early customers and generate real learning. MVP does not mean low quality, it means maximum learning for minimum investment. The question is not 'what is the smallest thing we can build?' but 'what is the smallest thing that will tell us if we're right?'
steps: Define the one core assumption your business depends on most.
Design an MVP that tests specifically that assumption, not all assumptions.
Set your learning criteria before building: what result would confirm or deny the assumption?

After shipping, treat every customer interaction as data, not validation. Dropbox never built the product first. They made a three-minute demo video showing how it would work and posted it online. Overnight signups went from 5,000 to 75,000. The MVP was a video, not code. They validated the assumption people want effortless file syncing, before writing a single line. IN PRACTICE
promptBody:
Act as a lean startup product advisor.
My business idea   :   [DESCRIBE IN 2–3 SENTENCES]
Core assumption   :   [THE ONE THING THAT MUST BE TRUE FOR THIS BUSINESS TO  
                                     WORK]
Step 1      :  What is the smallest product or experiment that tests this specific  
                    assumption?
Step 2     :  What does success look like? Define the metric or signal that confirms the 
                   assumption.
Step 3     :  What does failure look like? What result would tell me to pivot or stop?
Step 4     :  What is the fastest way to build or simulate this MVP,  even without writing 
                  code?
Be specific. Avoid suggesting a full product build.

proTip:
The most common MVP mistake is testing too many assumptions at once. One MVP, one
assumption. If it passes, move to the next assumption. Running MVP tests in sequence is
faster than building a complete product that tests them all at once and fails without
telling you which assumption was wrong.
